### 38. Evaluating an Agent
*Planned — estimate 14 pp.*

> My agent succeeded four times out of five. I don't know whether that is good.

Covers: A task, a trial and a grader; grading with code first, then models, then people; checking the final state and reading the transcript; pass@k against pass^k, with the arithmetic worked — 0.95 a step over 20 steps is 0.36; capability suites kept apart from regression suites that must stay near 100%

### 39. Adapting a Model: Prompt, Retrieve or Tune
*Planned — estimate 22 pp.*

> People keep asking whether I fine-tuned it. I don't know how to answer, or when I should.

Covers: Retrieval supplies knowledge, tuning changes behaviour; what it costs to own a tuned model; parameter-efficient fine-tuning and LoRA, with the parameter arithmetic; when *you* would do each stage and what it costs you (chapter 14 owns what the stages do); distillation into smaller models; side effects beyond the target task; releasing only behind an evaluation gate; synthetic data added to real data, never substituted

## Part III · Apply — 11 labs, 190 pp

### 40. Lab: Call a Model and Measure It
*Planned — estimate 20 pp.*

> I've read about tokens, cost and variance. I've never watched any of them happen.

Covers: A virtual environment, a pinned client and a key read from the environment; a first call; counting tokens both ways; measuring latency; the same prompt twenty times, and the spread

### 41. Lab: An Evaluation Set, and Two Prompts Compared Properly
*Planned — estimate 18 pp.*

> I have two prompts and a feeling. I want a number with an interval around it.

Covers: Thirty labelled cases on a task with an **exact-match grader**, so no judge is needed yet; both prompts over repeated trials; a bootstrap interval; a verdict you could defend

### 42. Lab: A Schema and One Tool
*Planned — estimate 16 pp.*

> I want output my code can trust, and one action the model can ask for but not take.

Covers: A JSON schema and a validation failure rate; one tool the model proposes; your code validating and refusing a bad call; a log of every proposal

### 43. Lab: Two Embedding Models, and the Query That Breaks Them
*Planned — estimate 16 pp.*

### 44. Lab: Hybrid Retrieval With a Reranker, Measured
*Planned — estimate 22 pp.*

### 45. Lab: The Pipeline End to End
*Planned — estimate 22 pp.*

### 46. Lab: Error Analysis, and a Judge You Can Trust
*Planned — estimate 18 pp.*

### 47. Lab: Workflow Against Agent
*Planned — estimate 12 pp.*

### 48. Lab: Context and Tools, Measured
*Planned — estimate 12 pp.*

### 49. Lab: Measure and Reduce Cost and Latency
*Planned — estimate 16 pp.*

> I know what the levers are. I have never pulled one and watched the number move.

Covers: Time to first token and time per token measured; the prompt reordered so the stable part comes first, and prefix caching measured; a cheap model routed to the easy cases, with quality checked; a cost per request before and after

### 50. Lab: Attack Your Own System
*Planned — estimate 18 pp.*

> If a document can tell my agent what to do, I'd rather find out myself.

Covers: An injected instruction in a retrieved document, a tool output and the memory store from lab 48; what the system does; the three attacks turned into a suite; **one `pytest` command that runs the regression set and the attack suite and prints the counts**

## Part IV · What Next — 7 chapters, 136 pp

### 51. Security: What Can Go Wrong, and What Limits the Damage
*Planned — estimate 36 pp.*

> Someone told me a web page could hijack my agent. I'd like to know whether that's true and what I do about it.

Covers: Why a model cannot reliably tell instructions from data; the current risk lists for agents and for applications that only generate, in tables; using a list as a checklist, not a certificate; the design rule — never combine untrusted input, sensitive access and external action in one session without approval; every channel the model reads being input; **insecure output handling**, where model output reaches HTML, SQL or a shell; **per-user tool authorisation**, so a tool acts with the caller's rights and not the service's; **sandboxing generated code**; third-party tool servers as supply chain; why filters and guardrails are never the only defence; attack suites that run on every change

### 52. Speed: What Makes This Slow
*Planned — estimate 24 pp.*

> My system is correct and nobody will wait for it.

Covers: What you measure and which lever you pull (chapter 15 owns why, from the inside): time to first token and time per token in production; what long context, reranking and agent loops add; prompt-prefix caching and ordering your prompt for it; routing and cascades; application-level response caching, which is not the provider's; if you serve models yourself — continuous batching, paged key--value cache, speculative decoding, quantisation; measuring on your own workload

### 53. Cost: What This Costs Me
*Planned — estimate 20 pp.*

> The bill arrived and I cannot account for it.

Covers: Paying for tokens in and out, including reasoning tokens; features that multiply usage — reasoning modes, multi-agent designs, long contexts; budgeting them instead of switching them on; the economics of caching and cascades; cost per request as a product constraint, measured against lab 49's baseline

### 54. Failure: How This Breaks, and How I Diagnose It
*Planned — estimate 26 pp.*

> It worked last week. Nothing in my code changed.

Covers: Attributing a failure with traces; pinned model versions and gated upgrades; a provider's update as a change that must pass your regression suite; versioning prompts, configuration, indexes and models as one artefact; **re-embedding and index migration when the embedding model changes**; provider data retention, and where your customers' text goes; gradual rollout; deciding in advance what triggers a rollback

### 55. A System Designed Aloud
*Planned — estimate 16 pp.*

> They will give me forty-five minutes and a whiteboard and say "design this". I have never had to say any of it out loud.

Covers: One whole system designed from a vague requirement, in the order an interview expects it: what to clarify first; the retrieval choice and why; the evaluation plan before the build; cost per request estimated on the back of an envelope; the failure modes named; what you would measure in week one; what you would not build yet. Reasoning spoken, not diagrammed

### 56. What to Learn Next
*Planned — estimate 8 pp.*

> I can hold a conversation about all of this now. I want to know what I actually don't know.

Covers: Where the theory begins — statistics, representation learning, retrieval and ranking, evaluation science; the standard books by chapter; reading one complete production system end to end; how to keep up without chasing announcements

### 57. What to Skip for Now
*Planned — estimate 6 pp.*

> Everything claims to be essential.

Covers: What an interview does not reach; what to postpone and why; the regress of prerequisites, and where to stop
